Coding-agent request flow (1.5 min)

We'll use a coding agent as our workload throughout the workshop. The agent runs outside the model server. It keeps track of the task, sends requests to the model, and runs any tools the model asks it to use.

[click] For the first request, the agent sends the code and the user's instructions to the server through the chat completions endpoint.

[click] The model returns a response. In this example, that response asks the agent to run a tool.

[click] The agent runs it and collects the result. That could be the contents of a file, some test output, or an error message.

[click] For the next request, the agent sends the earlier conversation again, with that tool result and any new instructions appended.

[click] This repeats until the task is complete. So one agent session can generate many inference requests, and successive requests contain a lot of the same text.

That repeated context is important for serving. The server needs to process the new material, but we'd like it to reuse work it has already done on the shared prefix. We'll first look at where that work happens and what the server needs to keep in memory.

fund:1:
LLM serving architecture (1.5 min)

On the server side, the request first reaches an HTTP endpoint. That's the interface the agent talks to, and it's also where the generated tokens stream back to the client.

[click] Behind that endpoint is vLLM. Its serving stack converts the prompt into token IDs, and the engine schedules the work that will run on the GPUs.

It uses continuous batching, so requests can join or leave the batch as execution progresses. The scheduler decides which requests can run together, within the available compute and memory limits.

The engine also manages the KV cache. This holds the attention state computed for tokens in the context, so later computation can reuse it. vLLM allocates that state in blocks as requests need space.

[click] The GPUs hold the model weights and the working memory, and execute the model's kernels. Their arithmetic throughput determines how quickly they can perform calculations. Their memory bandwidth determines how quickly they can supply the data those calculations need.

To see how those limits affect a request, we need to separate prompt processing from token generation.

fund:2:
Prefill and decode (1 min)

When the server handles a request, it first processes the prompt and then generates the response. We call those two phases prefill and decode.

[click] During prefill, the model processes the input tokens and builds their KV cache. It can work on many prompt tokens together. A longer uncached prompt gives it more work to do before the answer can begin.

That delay contributes to time to first token. From the client's point of view, this also includes any time the request spends waiting in a queue.

[click] During decode, the model generates the response one token at a time. Each step uses the existing context and adds the new token's state to the cache, ready for the next step.

The time between those tokens determines how quickly the answer arrives once it has started. If several requests are running together, the engine schedules their generation steps together too.

So we need to watch both the wait for the first token and the speed of generation after that. A serving configuration can improve one without improving the other.

fund:3:
GPU memory allocation (1.5 min)

GPU memory gives us a fixed budget, and the engine has to share it between the three uses shown here.

[click] First are the model weights. We load them when the worker starts, and every request uses that same copy. Adding another user doesn't require another copy of the weights.

[click] The engine also needs workspace to execute the model. That includes temporary activations and scratch buffers, along with memory for captured execution graphs when those are enabled. We have to allow room for this work before we decide how much cache the engine can support.

[click] The engine reserves part of the remaining memory for the KV-cache pool. This holds the attention state for the requests we're serving. As requests process more tokens, they need more blocks, so longer contexts use more of the pool.

[click] These users are all sharing that pool. We can fit more short requests, or fewer long ones, into the same amount of memory. If we keep adding requests, the engine eventually runs out of available blocks and has to make requests wait or reclaim space.

That's why memory is a serving budget. The weights determine part of the fixed cost, and the space left for KV cache helps determine how many requests we can keep active. More active requests can improve total throughput, but they also share the GPU's execution time, which can increase latency.

fund:4:
Memory tiers and bandwidth (1.5 min)

We can keep data in several places, but the GPU can't access all of them at the same speed. This chart compares the bandwidth available to read or move that data from each of them. The numbers are published hardware examples. Our workshop runs on H100s.

[click] On-chip SRAM provides very high bandwidth with limited capacity. GPUs use it for registers and caches. The Groq example here uses SRAM as its main working storage.

[click] HBM is the GPU memory we were just dividing up. It provides the capacity and bandwidth for model weights, execution buffers and active KV state.

[click] CPU memory gives us more space to retain cached context. Accessing that context requires data to cross the host-to-GPU connection, which takes time and consumes bandwidth.

[click] Flash storage adds more capacity again. It can hold checkpoints or retained context, but retrieving that data also depends on the storage system and the connection to it. The link rates shown here are limits, rather than measured storage read speeds.

[click] Another GPU may already have the data we need. A peer transfer can copy cached KV blocks or model weights directly between GPUs, using the available interconnect.

When we reuse cached state, its location matters. We save the work of recomputing it, but we may have to pay for a transfer. We'll use that tradeoff when we look at offloading and moving state between workers.

fund:5:
Prefix caching (1.5 min)

Let's return to the two requests from our agent. The first contains the code and the user's task.

[click] The second contains that same text, followed by the model's response and the tool result. Only the end of the request has changed.

[click] The server has already computed the KV state for the shared prefix. If those blocks are still cached, it can reuse them for this request. It doesn't need to run the same prompt tokens through prefill again.

[click] It then processes the new context at the end. Those new tokens still attend to the cached prefix, so the model continues to use the full context. We've avoided recomputing the earlier state.

Reuse requires a matching token prefix. For an agent that makes many turns over the same code, this can avoid substantial repeated work. But the request needs to reach a worker that can actually access the cached prefix.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• The reuse depends on a matching token prefix. If an application changes text near the start of the prompt, the engine can lose reuse for the tokens that follow it. Keeping repeated instructions and tool definitions consistent helps preserve that match.

fund:6:
Cache locality and prefill latency (1.5 min)

Here's what happens when we route that second request to either of two workers. Both run the same model, but their caches contain different state.

[click] Server A handled the first request and still has its prefix cached. It can reuse those blocks, process the new context and begin generating the next response.

[click] Server B has no matching prefix. It has to process the full context before it can start generating. The client sent the same request, but this worker has more GPU work to do.

That can increase time to first token and consume capacity that could have served other requests. The actual latency also depends on how busy each worker is. A cached prefix is useful, but waiting behind a long queue can offset that benefit.

[click] So request placement needs to consider both cached state and current load. Round-robin routing doesn't account for the difference we're showing here.

Dynamo can route a request toward reusable state, and KVCR can make state available on another worker by transferring it. We'll cover both later. First, let's deploy a worker and see how Dynamo exposes it as a service.

Worker startup latency (1.5 min)

Creating the worker Pod is only the beginning of startup. Before it can serve requests, the model has to be loaded and the engine has to be prepared.

[click] The bar separates three parts of that work. The first includes scheduling, image pulling and process startup. Loading the model means reading the checkpoint, preparing its tensors and copying them into GPU memory. The engine also has to allocate its cache and buffers, warm up kernels and, in this configuration, compile and capture CUDA graphs.

[click] In this recorded run, loading the weights took 267 seconds, and engine initialization took another 144. With the other startup work, the worker took eight minutes and thirteen seconds to become ready.

[click] These timings came from one run on two H100s, with the checkpoint on shared storage and compilation enabled. They'll vary with the deployment, but the breakdown shows why faster storage alone won't remove all of the delay.

That delay matters when we're adding capacity: the new worker can only take requests after startup finishes.

fund:10:
Inference performance metrics (1.5 min)

Once the worker is ready, we need to measure how it behaves under load. The timeline follows a request from the moment we send it until the last token arrives.

[click] Time to first token measures how long we wait before the response starts. That includes time in a queue as well as prompt processing and transport overhead.

[click] After the first token, we measure how quickly the rest arrive. Inter-token latency is the time between tokens. Tokens per second per user expresses generation speed as a rate.

[click] End-to-end latency covers the whole request, including that initial wait and the time to generate the answer. Longer answers can take more time even when generation speed stays the same.

[click] Throughput measures how much work the whole service completes, usually in output tokens or requests per second.

[click] We also count requests that fail, time out or finish without a complete response. A throughput increase is less useful if more requests fail.

We'll use these measurements together, because a configuration can produce more tokens overall while making each user wait longer.

Per-user token rate versus throughput (2.5 min)

This chart shows why we need both throughput and per-user generation speed when we compare serving configurations.

[click] Each point is a measured configuration for the model and hardware shown here. Moving right means faster generation for each user. Moving up means more output tokens per second for the same power budget.

Take the point near the bend as an example: a P90 per-user rate of about 418 tokens per second at 8.3 million output tokens per second per megawatt. The leftmost point delivers about five times that throughput at half the per-user rate.

Batching helps explain the tradeoff. Processing more requests together can make better use of the GPU, increasing total throughput. But as the batch grows, each step can take longer, so each user's answer arrives more slowly.

[click] The configurations toward the left favor throughput. They can suit offline evaluations or rollouts where we care about completing a large amount of work. Those toward the right favor faster responses for interactive users.

The choice depends on the workload's latency requirements. We first decide how fast generation needs to be for each user, then choose the highest-throughput configuration that meets that requirement.

We'll now increase the number of concurrent agents using the same deployment. To understand the resulting load, we need to follow the requests those agents produce.

scaling:2:
KV-cache capacity and CPU offloading (1.5 min)

As we add agents, more requests need space for their context. This brings us back to the GPU memory allocation we looked at earlier.

[click] In this example, the weights and workspace stay the same size, while the requests fill the KV-cache pool.

[click] When the engine runs out of blocks, it can reclaim unused cached prefixes, keep new requests waiting or preempt running requests. If useful cached state is removed, a later request may need to recompute it. Both waiting and recomputation can increase latency.

[click] CPU offloading gives us somewhere else to retain reusable blocks. If a GPU copy is evicted, the engine can fetch an available copy from host memory instead of recomputing that prefix.

The transfer still takes time and uses the CPU-to-GPU link. Whether it helps depends on how that transfer cost compares with the prefill work it avoids.

The model still executes on the same GPU. Offloading lets us retain more cached state and can reduce repeated computation, but requests continue to share the same execution capacity. To add more execution capacity, we can add another worker.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• If asked about routing to offloaded blocks: the workers must publish the corresponding cache events for the router to account for CPU-resident KV.

scaling:4:
Prefill and decode resource contention (2 min)

We've seen how to move cached state between workers. That also lets us run prefill and decode on different workers. To see why we'd do that, let's look at what happens when they share an engine.

[click] Prefill processes many prompt tokens together, so a large prefill can make heavy use of arithmetic throughput. Decode generates one token per active sequence at each step. At small batch sizes, reading the weights and KV cache often makes memory bandwidth the limiting factor. Those different demands give us a reason to tune the phases separately.

[click] In this timeline, A, B and C are already generating. Then request D arrives with a long prompt. The green block shows its prefill running as one uninterrupted step.

[click] While that step runs, A, B and C wait for their next tokens. Chunked prefill reduces this interruption by breaking the prompt into smaller pieces and interleaving decode. But the two phases still compete for the same GPU resources. Disaggregation gives each phase its own workers, so we can control their scheduling and capacity independently.

scaling:5:
Prefill and decode worker pools (1.5 min)

Here's what that separation looks like in a deployment.

[click] The client still sends its request to the frontend. The frontend coordinates the work across the two pools.

[click] The prefill workers process the prompt and produce the KV cache that decode will need. We can tune their parallelism and batching for the incoming prompt workload.

[click] The decode workers receive that cache over NIXL and generate the response. They have their own model weights and their own KV-cache capacity for active sequences. The tokens stream back through the frontend.

The diagram uses different tensor-parallel sizes to show that the pools can have different configurations. Those sizes are examples. The right settings depend on the model and workload.

[click] We can also change the number of workers in each pool independently. More incoming prompt work may require more prefill workers. Longer outputs or more concurrent generations may require more decode workers. We can even use different GPU types where the backend supports that configuration. The useful change is that we can allocate capacity to whichever phase needs it.

scaling:6:
Disaggregated request flow (2 min)

Let's follow one request through the vLLM layout shown here.

[click] The agent sends its request to the frontend, which handles preprocessing and routing.

[click] The prefill worker processes the uncached part of the prompt. If it already has a matching prefix, it can reuse that state. It then returns metadata identifying the KV blocks and the worker that holds them.

[click] The frontend forwards that metadata with the request, so the decode worker can locate the state it needs. The KV-cache payload then moves between the workers.

[click] The decode worker allocates local cache blocks and uses NIXL to fetch the remote blocks into its GPU memory. In our cross-node demo, that transfer uses LIBFABRIC over EFA. The configured transport and available network devices matter here.

[click] Once the required cache is available, decode generates tokens and streams them back to the agent. A transfer can overlap compute for other requests, but this request's generation depends on its own cache being ready. That dependency is why the transfer path affects time to first token.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• This describes the vLLM pull path in the slide. Worker-selection and coordination order can differ across backends and releases.

scaling:7:
Disaggregation performance (1.5 min)

There are three ways this separation can improve performance.

[click] First, a long prefill runs on different GPUs from ongoing decode. That reduces the interference we saw in the timeline. Each pool can still queue work, and they can still compete for network bandwidth.

[click] Second, we can tune parallelism and batching separately. Prefill wants low tensor parallelism and token-heavy batches. Decode wants high tensor parallelism and many concurrent sequences. One engine has to pick a compromise between them; two pools do not.

[click] Third, we can size each pool for the work it actually receives. Prefill demand follows the uncached prompt tokens. Decode demand depends on how many sequences are active, how much context they have, and how long their outputs are. We need measurements of both to choose the replica counts.

[click] How much this helps depends on the workload. Long prompts, long outputs and high concurrency benefit most. The practical test is whether disaggregation meets our latency target more efficiently for the workload we intend to serve.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• The local Super VL result is a fixed-order, single-run observation. Repeated load sweeps are required for a capacity claim.

Dynamo disaggregation configuration (1.5 min)

In the DGD, we keep the frontend and define separate worker services for prefill and decode.

[click] This service runs in prefill mode and has its own replica count.

[click] The other service runs in decode mode. In our demo, both use the same model revision and compatible cache settings, with two GPUs per worker. The workers also need the shared memory and transport devices required by their runtime. Our cross-node configuration uses EFA for NIXL transfers.

[click] We can apply the same idea to multimodal inference by separating image encoding from the language-model work. Encoder workers produce embeddings and pass them over NIXL. That can reduce interference for image-heavy traffic. The improvement shown here comes from a specific image workload and depends on how the encoder workers are placed.

[click] In the workshop demo, we'll check that prefill and decode run on distinct workers and that NIXL transfers complete. That verifies the serving path. Measuring its capacity requires repeated runs at increasing load, so we can see where each pool starts to queue.

Once we have separate pools, we also need a way to adjust their sizes as traffic changes. That's what the Planner does.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• Run the disaggregation demonstration after the fourth click. Verify separate worker identities and completed NIXL transfers in the logs and metrics.

• The demo uses TP2 in both pools, 64-token blocks, matching attention and recurrent-state layouts, and LIBFABRIC over EFA. Do not imply automatic TCP fallback.

• The encoder benchmark used Qwen3.5 122B NVFP4 with 10 images and 1,024 output tokens. Reported TTFT reductions were 58% with colocated encoders and 50% with a separate GPU tier; the separate tier added GPUs.

scaling:10:
Dynamo Planner (1.5 min)

As traffic changes, prefill and decode won't necessarily need to grow at the same rate. Dynamo's Planner automates those replica decisions.

[click] It reads traffic and engine metrics, including queued tokens, batch composition and execution time. These describe more than how many requests arrived. A request with a long prompt or a long output creates a different amount of work from a short one.

[click] The configured policy turns those signals into target replica counts. It can use load thresholds, or it can use a performance model to estimate the capacity needed for latency targets. Prefill and decode get separate counts, within the configured limits.

[click] The Kubernetes connector writes those counts into the DGD. The Dynamo operator reconciles the change and creates or removes the worker pods.

[click] So the Planner decides how much capacity to request, while the operator creates the resources. A new worker still has to start and become ready before it can serve traffic. That startup delay matters when we choose how early to scale. We're scaling manually in this workshop. The next slide explains the two scaling policies.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• No live Planner demonstration is scheduled. This slide explains the configured architecture; workshop replica changes are manual.

• Do not imply that Planner scale-down always drains in-flight requests. The behavior depends on the deployment path and version.

planner:4:
Planner scaling policies (1.5 min)

We choose between these two approaches with the Planner's optimization target setting.

On the left, we scale from engine load. The Planner checks queued prefill tokens and decode KV demand. That demand can include queued work, which is why the scale can go above a hundred percent. It isn't simply the fraction of physical cache blocks occupied.

The throughput preset tolerates more queueing before adding capacity. The latency preset scales earlier. With the load policy, we choose the scale-up and scale-down thresholds ourselves. By default, these checks run every five seconds.

On the right, SLA mode starts from latency targets. In this example, we want time to first token within five hundred milliseconds and inter-token latency within fifty milliseconds.

The forecast loop runs every three minutes by default and sets a minimum replica count for predicted demand. We can also enable a reactive loop that checks every five seconds and can adjust the count by one replica. It uses latency estimates from engine metrics and the performance model, so we still need to check the actual latency our clients experience.

These targets guide scaling decisions. Whether we meet them depends on the workload, available capacity and how quickly new workers become ready.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• This slide has no manual animation steps; do not add CLICK cues.

• The spoken name 'optimization target' refers to the optimization_target field. SLA mode is optimization_target: sla; the optional reactive loop is enable_load_scaling.

• Default loop intervals are 5 seconds for load checks and 180 seconds for the SLA predictive loop. Preset thresholds are version-specific.

router:15:
Request admission and overload protection (1.5 min)

When requests arrive faster than the workers can finish them, the queue grows and requests spend longer waiting. We may still be generating plenty of tokens, while more requests miss their latency target.

The chart compares accepting all that work with limiting what reaches the workers. Goodput here counts requests that meet the time-to-first-token target. As offered load passes capacity, the illustration shows goodput falling without admission control. With admission control, excess work waits or gets rejected, keeping the admitted requests within the target.

This is an illustration. The two-second target and eighty-percent admission limit are settings for this chart. A real deployment needs limits based on its measured performance.

The four mechanisms below give us different controls. We can reject a request when all eligible workers are busy. Dynamo's default overload response is HTTP 529. We can hold requests in policy-class queues, then use deficit round robin to share service between those classes, accounting for their weights and uncached input tokens.

Finally, a classifier can admit, defer or reject a request before it enters the router queue. We'll use that last mechanism to make decisions across an agent's whole session.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• Move the offered-load slider from below 100% to above 100% while discussing the chart. This is an interactive control, not a deck-progress CLICK cue.

• Worker-busy thresholds must be configured. Queue limits and ordering are configurable; deficit round robin arbitrates between classes, while ordering within each class is a separate policy.

• HTTP 529 does not implement client retries. Clients need an appropriate backoff or alternate-endpoint policy.

• The classifier runs before the router queue. In a disaggregated topology, remote prefill may have begun earlier, so avoid claiming it always runs before any inference work.

router:31:
Request-level routing and session memory (1.5 min)

Remember the agent loop from the start of the workshop: the model answers, the agent runs a tool, and then it sends another request with the accumulated context. The inference request ends at each turn, but that context can still be useful on the next one.

That's what the rows on the left show. Some agents are generating and others are running tools. Their cached prefixes can remain in GPU memory between turns. With similarly sized contexts, the total working set grows roughly with the number of sessions times the context per session, before accounting for shared prefixes.

Dynamo's KV router considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing each request. That helps reuse the cache, but it doesn't reserve enough space for every session's future turns.

If useful context exceeds cache capacity, blocks get evicted. When those sessions return, the missing prefixes need prefill again. Under enough load, we're spending more compute rebuilding context that we already processed.

Session-aware admission gives us another option: let the current model turn finish, then hold the session's next request. We can limit the sessions competing for cache without interrupting a generation already in progress.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• Cached prefixes are evictable, not permanently reserved. A cache miss may be partial; full eviction requires a full prefill.

• The rough N × context estimate excludes shared-prefix reuse. Available host or remote cache tiers can also change the amount of recomputation.

• All content enters automatically; this slide has no deck-progress click steps.

router:32:
Session-aware admission (1.5 min)

Dynamo's experimental ThunderAgent plugin adds that session-level decision inside the frontend. It groups requests by session ID and uses their token counts to estimate how much context each session carries.

The table separates two questions. The rows describe what the session is doing. In the reasoning row, a model turn is pending or running. In the acting row, the model turn has finished and control is back with the agent, often while a tool runs.

The columns describe whether the scheduler is allowing that session to continue. An active session's next request can proceed. A paused session's next request waits, while any external tool work can continue.

Under memory pressure, the scheduler first pauses sessions that are already between model turns. If that isn't enough, it can mark running sessions to pause when their current turn finishes. It doesn't stop decode halfway through an answer.

Pausing changes what the scheduler admits. The engine still decides when cached blocks are reused or evicted. When the estimated demand falls, the scheduler can resume sessions that fit on the available workers. The next slide shows how it makes that capacity decision.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• The native plugin runs inside the frontend and is experimental. This script describes that implementation, not the older standalone Python router.

• ACTING means the model turn has completed; it is not direct instrumentation of every external tool's lifecycle.

• Session token counts are logical accounting, not measurements of physical KV blocks. Admission state is local to the plugin instance.

• Selection favors smaller contexts within each admission group; do not describe it as an unconditional globally smallest-first policy.

router:33:
Session utilization and admission thresholds (1.5 min)

For each worker, the scheduler adds up the token counts of its active sessions, including a buffer for each one, and divides that by the GPU's KV-cache capacity in tokens. Active includes sessions that are generating and sessions between turns.

That gives us the utilization estimate at the top. It's an estimate of the context we're allowing to stay active. It can differ from physical memory use because sessions may share prefixes or have cache stored elsewhere.

The three markers show the default thresholds. Above ninety-five percent, the scheduler starts pausing smaller sessions that are between turns, aiming to bring the estimate down to eighty percent. If necessary, it also marks running sessions to pause after their current turn.

A paused session leaves that active estimate. Its cached bytes can still be present until the engine reuses the space, so the number can fall before physical memory use changes.

To resume a session normally, its context and buffer must fit while keeping projected utilization below eighty-five percent. That leaves a gap below the pause threshold, reducing the chance that we immediately pause it again. The scheduler uses those estimates to select sessions and place them on workers with enough headroom.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• Native defaults: pause when U > 0.95; pause toward 0.80; normal resume requires projected U < 0.85, using a 0.10 gap below the pause threshold.

• The utilization estimate includes ACTIVE reasoning and acting programs plus per-program token buffers. The implementation can weight acting programs. Its denominator is GPU KV capacity, not GPU plus host offload capacity.

• Worker pinning constrains placement. Resume selects candidates within admission groups and packs the selected programs across workers.

• The footer describes a separate default 30-minute deferral timeout. It releases a waiting request when a worker is live; downstream queues, eligibility and client deadlines still apply. It does not guarantee an end-to-end completion deadline.

• There are no native Python-prototype soft-demotion or one-second priority-boost controls in this implementation.

router:34:
Session scheduling benchmark results (1.5 min)

These are two reported evaluations, each with its own model, hardware and baseline. On the left, the SWE-bench workload gained twelve to sixteen percent throughput over KV-aware routing alone.

The table on the right shows why concurrency matters. At thirty-two to a hundred and twenty-eight concurrent RL rollouts, throughput was similar to the baseline. At a hundred and ninety-two to two hundred and fifty-six, model-token throughput was eleven to fourteen-point-six percent higher. At the highest concurrency levels, the baseline's throughput dropped sharply while the session-aware scheduler's throughput continued to rise.

The reported prefix-cache hit rate stayed above ninety-four-point-five percent across that RL sweep. That is the behavior this policy is trying to preserve: enough useful context remains available that later turns can reuse it, leaving more compute for new work.

For a deployment, we would measure throughput and latency across increasing session concurrency, alongside cache reuse and repeated prefill. That tells us whether session admission helps with our workload and how much waiting it introduces.

We've now covered how to add capacity, divide it between prefill and decode, and control the work we admit. Next, we'll look at what happens when workers fail.

Presenter instructions and reference details (not spoken):

• Reported by Dynamo's October 8, 2026 evaluation, not independently rerun here.

• Left: MiniMax-M2, two TP4 replicas on one eight-H100 node, SWE-bench; comparison is against KV-aware routing alone.
